title: Module 2 · Lesson 1 — Tool design: the contract between model and system

lines: Lesson one is tool design.
It's the contract between a model and the system it drives.
Picture a plant shop whose support agent has two tools, both described as search.
A customer asks where her fern is, and the agent searches the product catalogue.
The team wants a bigger model.
But a vague tool is far more often the cause than a weak model.
The model never runs anything itself.
It emits a request: a tool name, plus JSON arguments matching a declared schema.
Your runtime validates, authorises, and runs it, then returns the result as an observation.
That split underpins every security control in an agent.
A strict JSON Schema lets code reject a malformed call before it runs.
The error goes back to the model, which can correct itself.
The schema also lets providers constrain decoding, so arguments are valid by construction.
And enums, limits, and formats describe valid values better than prose.

say.1: And eenums, limits, and formats describe valid values better than prose.

lines: The description is a prompt, read just as the model picks a tool.
Say what it does, when to use it, when not to, and what it returns.
So the shop adds negative scope: order lookup is for a customer's own orders.
Do not use it for products; use product search instead.
Too many similar tools blur together, yet one giant tool with a mode switch just moves the confusion into an argument.
So climb a ladder: sharper descriptions, merge or split, group, retrieve, then sub-agents.
Then a refund call times out after the refund went through, and the agent retries.
An idempotency key, which the server deduplicates on, means the customer is refunded only once.

say.1: An idem-potency key, which the server deduplicates on, means the customer is refunded only once.

lines: Separate read and write tools, and put destructive ones behind human approval.
And make errors actionable: "expected YYYY-MM-DD" lets the model fix itself, while "400 Bad Request" does not.

say.1: And make errors actionable: expected year, month, day, lets the model fix itself, while four hundred, bad request, does not.

lines: Authorisation belongs in the tool, never in the system prompt.
Check the user's permissions on every call, the only defence that survives prompt injection.
Exam trap: strict typing does not eliminate hallucination, because it guarantees a well-formed call, not the right one.
Read on for the full tool-design checklist.
